report.source_text: A 46-year-old staff nurse presented to an emergency doctor on 12 April 2020 with a 24-hour history of a widespread red-raised blanching and itchy rash. Her partner had just recovered from presumed COVID-19 infection; having only had mild symptoms, she was not tested and was back at work. Our patient was on day 13 of self-isolation and was hoping to return to work the following day. She had no fever or continuous cough but did have some nasal congestion. The patient had a history of hay fever, a possible nut allergy and mild asthma. She had not been prescribed any regular medications and had not taken any over-the-counter medications; she had no known allergies to medications. The general practitioner described a classical urticarial rash affecting her upper and lower limbs in addition to her trunk. A diagnosis of probable idiopathic urticaria was suggested and the patient was prescribed fexofenadine hydrochloride 180 mg, to be taken two to four times per day.

clinician.final_diagnosis: Reverse transcriptase PCR test on combined nasopharyngeal/oropharyngeal swabs was positive for SARS-CoV-2, 2 days after first presenting to the emergency doctor.
clinician.trajectory_summary: A 46-year-old staff nurse presented on April 12, 2020, with a widespread red-raised blanching and itchy rash and nasal congestion, initially diagnosed as probable idiopathic urticaria. The following day, April 13, 2020, her rash worsened, and she developed new symptoms including swelling of lips and hands, feverishness, and a dry cough. A GP advised self-isolation and suggested SARS-CoV-2 testing. Two days after initial presentation, on April 14, 2020, a reverse transcriptase PCR test on combined nasopharyngeal/oropharyngeal swabs was positive for SARS-CoV-2. The patient was treated with fexofenadine, prednisolone, and chlorphenamine, and the rash resolved completely over the next few days, leading to a full clinical recovery.
